title: Private VPC networking deep dive - runtime, KV cache, batching
summary: Redwood SE walked through recommended Private VPC networking architecture for private deployments (PrivateLink, VPC endpoints, NAT, route tables, split-horizon DNS). Discussed performance implications for runtime: cross-AZ latency, egress hops, KV cache locality, batching impacts, and quantization tradeoffs. Customer asked about security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO) and benchmarking steps. Agreed next steps: share security pack, provide network diagram + sample Terraform, run a 24h benchmark runbook, and schedule on-site POC planning call.
next_steps: Redwood to share security documentation (SOC2 + architecture notes) by 2027-08-11
Omar to provide sample Terraform for VPC endpoints and PrivateLink by 2027-08-12
Customer to provision test VPC and confirm subnets by 2027-08-18
Schedule 24h benchmark run (latency & throughput) with Crestline infra week of 2027-08-23

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining our private VPC deep dive. We have Maya and Omar from Redwood, Priya is on for product context.
[00:07] Dana Moore: Hey thanks, we're excited — want to focus on networking and runtime tradeoffs for our on-premish VPC deployment.
[00:12] Omar Ruiz: Great, quick agenda: PrivateLink/Private endpoints, NAT/egress, DNS split-horizon, then how those affect latency, KV cache locality, batching and quant profiles.
[00:22] Ravi Kumar: Quick note on our setup — we have 3 AZs in us-east-1, internal only subnets for compute, a separate dedicated infra account, and SSO via Okta.
[00:30] Omar: Perfect. For Redwood Private we typically recommend placing the inference hosts in private subnets with access to a control plane through PrivateLink. That avoids open internet egress and gives consistent routing.
[00:40] Sofia Martinez: How does PrivateLink work with our SAML SSO and KMS? Any additional subnet rules?
[00:47] Omar: PrivateLink is just a VPC endpoint to Redwood's control plane or a customer-managed control plane (depending on architecture). SSO is independent — SAML goes through your IdP to the control plane over the private endpoint. For KMS, we support using your KMS keys; traffic to KMS typically goes via AWS endpoint or over a peering/VPN route, so you'll want a dedicated route for the KMS region.
[01:05] Dana: When you say "control plane" is that in our VPC or in Redwood's managed VPC?
[01:10] Maya: Two models — managed (Redwood control plane with PrivateLink) or self-hosted control plane in your account. For high-regulatory customers many choose the self-hosted control plane so logs and metadata never leave their account.
[01:20] Lee Park: We're leaning toward self-hosted control plane. Concerned about latency if the runtime is separated or if the control plane is in different AZs.
[01:28] Omar: Good point. Control plane traffic is low bandwidth and not latency critical. The runtime — where model inference happens — should be co-located in the same AZs as your compute to keep KV cache hits and inter-node latencies low. Cross-AZ hops add ~1-2 ms typically, which adds up for multi-token generation.
[01:42] Ravi: Can you quantify the performance hit for cross-AZ KV cache misses?
[01:46] Omar: On our tests, a local KV hit is sub-millisecond for a token, cross-AZ can add 1-3 ms depending on AZ pair; if you have 512 tokens average response that's additional 500-1500 ms in pathological batching scenarios. But usually with batching and local cache warm-up the amortized per-token impact is less.
[02:05] Priya Singh: Also note, KV cache effectiveness depends on request fanout and session affinity. We recommend sticky routing to keep sessions on the same host to maximize KV cache hits.
[02:15] Dana: Sticky routing — do you support that in the routing policy?
[02:18] Maya: Yes, routing policies can be session-affinity based, by token range, or latency-first. For Private deployments customers often pick affinity to preserve cache locality.
[02:28] Ravi: About NAT and egress: we want to limit internet egress and route only necessary traffic. How does Redwood handle model downloads and updates?
[02:35] Omar: Models can be pre-pulled into your private registry or we can ship them via a private S3 endpoint. Model downloads happen during deploy windows — those flows can use a specific NAT gateway route or a VPC endpoint to your S3. For runtime calls we recommend no internet egress — everything via PrivateLink.
[02:50] Sofia: Does that mean we need NAT for KMS calls?
[02:53] Omar: If you use AWS KMS and call the AWS public KMS endpoint, yes unless you configure the AWS KMS VPC endpoint. Many customers provision a KMS VPC endpoint or route those calls through a secure egress (transit gateway) to avoid NAT.
[03:05] Lee: DNS — we're running split-horizon DNS across accounts. Any gotchas with PrivateLink and internal DNS names?
[03:11] Omar: PrivateLink exposes an endpoint DNS hostname that resolves to a private IP in your VPC. If you're using split-horizon, ensure the private zone has precedence and that your resolvers forward correctly. We also recommend local resolver caching and TTL tuning to avoid resolution latency on bursts.
[03:27] Dana: What about throughput sizing and subnet sizing? We're planning 8 GPU nodes per AZ.
[03:31] Priya: For throughput, important levers are batch size, concurrency, and the number of runtime workers per GPU. Subnet-wise, ensure enough IPs for autoscaling (ECS/EKS nodes or k8s pods). We usually recommend a /20 per AZ for larger POCs to avoid exhaustion.
[03:45] Ravi: Batch sizing — we worry about tail latency when batch grows. How do you balance batching for cost vs p99 latency?
[03:51] Omar: Continuous batching in the runtime adapts to incoming qps; you can set SLOs to cap batch wait time. There is a tradeoff: bigger batches improve GPU utilization and lower tokens cost, but increase p95/p99. Our recommended pattern is target average batch sizes with a max latency cap (e.g., 50ms window). We'll show you tuning knobs in the runbook.
[04:10] Dana: Quantization — is that supported and does it change CPU/GPU memory footprint?
[04:14] Omar: Yes, Redwood supports int8 and hybrid quant profiles. Quantization reduces GPU memory and increases throughput in many models but can incur slight quality regression; we recommend A/B tests. Quantized kernels also behave differently on different hardware — we select kernels at runtime.
[04:28] Lee: Any implications for KV cache when using quantized models?
[04:31] Omar: KV cache format is orthogonal to quant — cache is model-specific but stored as dense float buffers; quantization affects compute kernels but caches are unquantized to preserve precision, though we have an option to compress caches. That said, cache size and network transfer for cache sync is a consideration for cross-node replication.
[04:48] Priya: For private clusters we recommend local cache + sticky sessions to avoid cache sync traffic. If you need cross-node sync, use it sparingly and prefer warm-starting popular flows.
[04:58] Ravi: Benchmarks — what's the best way to validate latency/throughput in our VPC?
[05:02] Omar: We'll provide a 24-hour benchmark runbook: synthetic traffic with your prompt mixes, simulate session stickiness, collect token-level latency, p50/p95/p99, and cost per 1M tokens. Run benchmarks with different quant levels and batching configs. The runbook will include Terraform to spin up test VPC endpoints.
[05:20] Sofia: Security questions: audit logs, retention, and where logs land in self-hosted model?
[05:25] Maya: In self-hosted control plane, logs can be delivered to your S3/CloudWatch and we can integrate with your SIEM. Audit trail of token metadata is configurable; content-level data handling we recommend tokenization redaction if needed. We also support customer-managed KMS/HSM for key storage.
[05:40] Dana: Any known issues with Transit Gateway setups across accounts?
[05:44] Omar: Transit Gateway works, but watch for routing complexity and additional hops. Each extra hop adds latency; for latency-sensitive inference you prefer direct VPC endpoints or peering within the same region/AZ. Transit gateway introduces centralized egress which can be fine for management but may cost extra latency.
[05:59] Lee: For failover, do you support multi-region deployments?
[06:02] Priya: Yes, we support routing policies to failover to a warm regional pool. The caveat: cross-region failover will increase latency and may change model variants if capacity differs. We recommend active-active in two regions for critical workloads.
[06:15] Ravi: Pricing — rough delta between hosted and private with dedicated GPUs?
[06:19] Maya: Private has a baseline infra fee plus per-GPU allowances; dedicated Reserved capacity reduces per-token cost. We'll send a pricing range in the security pack.
[06:27] Dana: Can you summarize recommended network architecture for us?
[06:30] Omar: Sure: 1) Place runtimes in private subnets across AZs, 2) Use PrivateLink endpoints for control-plane calls, 3) Use VPC endpoints for S3/KMS to avoid NAT, 4) Enable session-affinity routing to preserve KV cache hits, 5) Ensure resolver caching for PrivateLink DNS, and 6) provision /20-ish subnets for POC scale.
[06:50] Ravi: Any automation examples?
[06:52] Omar: We'll share Terraform modules for the endpoints, route tables, and sample node groups. That's part of the deliverables.
[06:58] Dana: OK great. Let's talk about a concrete POC plan — what's realistic scope?
[07:02] Maya: 4-week POC: week1 infra and endpoint provisioning; week2 deploy runtime + smoke tests; week3 run 24h performance runs; week4 analyze results and tune batching/quant. Deliverables: network diagram, Terraform, benchmark reports, and recommended config.
[07:18] Sofia: For compliance we'll need SOC2 docs and encryption details now.
[07:21] Maya: We'll attach our compliance pack; Omar will include KMS/HSM integration notes.
[07:26] Ravi: On the runtime side — are there any recommended kernel settings for our GPU type (A100 80GB)?
[07:31] Omar: A100 80GB is great for large models. We'll default to fused attention kernels and bfloat16/int8 profiles for throughput. We'll provide recommended batch/concurrency knobs per model and produce a quickstart perf table.
[07:45] Priya: Also call out cold-start behavior and warm-up scripts — pre-warming KV cache and model warms reduces p99 dramatically.
[07:53] Lee: Anything else on DNS?
[07:54] Omar: Just one more: ensure that your internal resolvers have low TTLs for endpoint rotation during failover tests, and that service discovery maps to the PrivateLink hostnames.
[08:06] Dana: Perfect, thanks. We'll look for the security pack and Terraform.
[08:09] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and scheduling.
[08:12] [meeting ends]
